0055.event: The Second Party tells of new footprints found beside the famous Laetoli trails. Perhaps the same day, perhaps the next, more walkers crossed the ash: a second large one, and another small one, following the same route. Read the ground like a letter and it says the plain held more than three. Two families, or one band that would not end at three. A people, moving through the morning together. The white plain kept every step, and the steps say what the bones alone cannot: that we go together, or we do not go far. The walkers were already social, already bound to one another, long before they were human in any other way.
0055.announce: What follows is the story of two families: The Second Party.
0055.title: The Second Party
0055.piece:
Later, maybe that same day, maybe the next, new prints appeared beside the first ones. A second large walker. Another small one. The same ash, the same direction, the same morning business of going somewhere.
Two families now, or one band that would not end at three. The plain was white and kept them all. Read the ground like a letter from old friends: me, and her, and you, and the little ones stepping in the deep.
Not three walkers anymore. A law, written in feet: we go together, or we do not go far.

0056.event: Little Foot is the nickname of the most complete ancient skeleton ever found. Deep in the Sterkfontein caves of South Africa, inside cold limestone, lies a climber-walker curled in stone, kept almost whole. The bones suggest a creature that both climbed and walked, at home in the trees and on the ground. It seems to have fallen down a deep shaft in the dark, a misstep it could not see, and the cave kept it. For millions of years it slept in the endless night, no torch ever lit above it. When it was found, it gave us more of one ancient body than any other fossil: proof, held in a single frame, of the in-between life our family once lived.
0056.announce: Listen to a verse for the one who fell: Little Foot.
0056.title: Little Foot
0056.piece:
Deep in the limestone, where the dark is old,
a skeleton lies curled inside the cold.
The most complete we ever found, kept whole,
a climber-walker, body and soul.
It fell, it seems, down a shaft unseen,
a misstep in the dark, the long drop clean.
The cave is strong. The cave keeps all.
No triumph here, just the soft fall.
No torch was lit above that night.
It sleeps in stone, out of the light.

0057.event: The Man-Stride is about a stride any human would recognize. In Ethiopia, the fossil trails of Australopithecus afarensis show the same order of motion our own feet use: heel down first, the weight rolling to the arch, the push of the toe, the swing, the next step. Above, the body was still ape: long arms, a climber's grip, a heavy brow. Below, the feet were us. Match your stride to theirs and the million years fall away, because the rhythm is the same and it always stays. The stride was human before we were fully human. An ape's arms, a climber's hold, and walking exactly like we walk now.
0057.announce: Here is a poem about the stride we still use: The Man-Stride.
0057.title: The Man-Stride
0057.piece:
Heel, arch, push. Heel, arch, push.
The prints spell out the stride in stone:
the body's frame was ape above,
but below, the feet were all our own.
Heel down first, the weight rolls to the toe,
the push, the swing. That much we know
by heart, by bone, by every mile.
The rhythm hasn't changed its style.
An ape's arms, a climber's grip, a brow
like night, and walking just like us now.

0058.event: The Flat-Faced One tells of a crushed skull found in Kenya with a face like no other. It did not jut forward the way ape faces do. It was flat, with small teeth at the front, a different answer to the old question of how to eat the savanna's hardness. Here was a second kind of walker, sharing the lakes and the plains with its cousins, living under the same high sky. The earth was trying more than one way to make us. Only one line would see the later ages. But on that day, at that shore, both drank, both lived, both wanted more. Difference is old. The family tried many shapes before it settled on ours.
0058.announce: A portrait in verse of the flat-faced one: The Flat-Faced One.
0058.title: The Flat-Faced One
0058.piece:
The skull was crushed, but the face was flat,
not jutting like the others. Small teeth at
the front gave a new answer to the game
of eating: grind it different, stake a claim
on roots and seeds the others left behind.
Two kinds of walkers, and both were kind
to the same lakes, the same wide sky.
The earth tried twice. We wonder why
only one line walked on. But then,
both drank that day. Both were kin.

0059.event: The Laetoli of the East tells of footprints found in the Afar region of Ethiopia, pressed into volcanic ash like the famous trails of Laetoli far to the south. Here too the ash fell, and here too feet went through it, leaving fresh proof that the two-legged walk had spread. Not one plain, not one trail, but a whole country learning to stand up. The prints point every way at once: north, south, toward water, into the scrub. They went wherever feet could go. The walking had won, and it was not a local habit. It was the way of East Africa, from the highlands to the coast, and it would not be given up.
0059.announce: Now a song about footprints across a country: The Laetoli of the East.
0059.title: The Laetoli of the East
0059.piece:
In Afar the ash fell too, soft and grey,
and feet went through it on their way.
Not one plain now, not one trail,
but a whole land learning without fail
to stand, to stride, to walk upright.
The prints point north, the prints point south,
each one a step from foot to mouth
of time. They went where feet could go.
The walking won. The walking said hello.

0060.event: The Burtele Foot is a fossil foot with a thumb for a big toe. Found in Ethiopia, it walked, but its big toe still grasped like a hand, built for the branch even as the rest of the foot moved on the ground. Not every road was the same song. Some of our cousins kept the trees as a way of life: the grip, the climb, the branch above the trouble of the open ground. They walked, but they could leave, up into the green where the leopards lost their prey. Two answers to the same fear: walk the plain, or keep the treetops near. The earth was large enough for more than one way to live.
0060.announce: A short story of the foot that kept the trees: The Burtele Foot.
0060.title: The Burtele Foot
0060.piece:
This foot had a thumb for a big toe. A grasping thing, built for the branch, although the rest of it walked. Hold that thought: not every road was the same song.
Some kept the trees as a way of life. The grip, the climb, the branch above the trouble of the open ground. They walked, but they could leave, up into green where the leopards lost their prey.
Two answers to the fear. Walk the plain, or keep the treetops near. I do not know which was wiser. Both were true. The earth was large enough for more than one way to live.

0061.event: The Stone Breakers tells of the oldest tools ever found. At Lomekwi in Kenya, someone picked up one stone and struck it against another, and the flake flew free: a sharp edge where none used to be. These broken rocks are about three million three hundred thousand years old, hundreds of thousands of years older than any tools we knew before. Older than the tale we told ourselves about when making began. Stone on stone. The first blow. The sound stays: hit it right, and the rock gives you an edge. Before the sail, before the wheel, before the word, there was a smashed rock, the sharpest thing the world had heard.
0061.announce: Hear the first blow fall, in verse: The Stone Breakers.
0061.title: The Stone Breakers
0061.piece:
Stone on stone.
The first blow.
At Lomekwi, hands learned
what rock could know.
Hit it right,
the flake flies free.
A sharp edge
where none used to be.
Three million years
before the wheel,
before the sail,
before the word was real:
a smashed rock,
the sharpest sound.
Stone on stone.
The world turned round.

0062.event: Anvils of the River tells of stones worn by work. Along ancient rivers in Kenya lie great cobbles, round and grey, pitted where hammer stones fell again and again. Thump, thump, the long work of the day: cracking nuts, cracking marrow bones, the crack, the scoop, the rich fat stirred. No poetry in it, just the daily bread, the pits in stone, the hands that never rest. But every nut they cracked was practice for the hands that would build everything after. The river keeps the anvils still, round and worn and waiting, the oldest workbenches in the world.
0062.announce: A work song for the river stones that fed them: Anvils of the River.
0062.title: Anvils of the River
0062.piece:
The river stones are round and worn and grey,
and pitted where the hammer stones fell.
Thump, thump, the long work of the day,
cracking the nuts, the marrow as well.
No poetry in it, just the daily bread,
the pits in stone, the hands that never rest.
But every flake they struck, each nut they fed,
was practice for the hands that built the best
of us. The river keeps the anvils still.
They wait there now. They always will.

0063.event: The Marked Rib is a fossil rib with thin, straight, deliberate lines cut across it. Not tooth marks, not weathering: the marks of sharp stone. Someone sliced meat from this bone while the world was waking to the taste. Run a finger down the ancient cuts and you hear not the knife but the mind behind the hand, learning to find food in the bone. The rib keeps score. Long before anyone wrote a word, the cuts said: we were here, we were hungry, and we had learned to eat in a new way. The stone had taught the hand, and the hand had taught the belly.
0063.announce: A tale cut into bone, in a short verse: The Marked Rib.
0063.title: The Marked Rib
0063.piece:
A rib. A fossil rib.
And on it, lines,
thin, straight, deliberate.
Cut marks. Signs
that sharp stone did this,
that meat was taken.
Someone sliced the flesh
while the world was waken
to a new taste. I ran
my finger down the cuts
and heard the mind behind
the hand: learn what the bone
can give. The rib keeps score.
We learned to eat. We wanted more.

0064.event: Lucy is the most famous ancestor of all. They called her Dinkinesh, which means you are marvelous, and marvelous she was. About three million two hundred thousand years ago, a young female walked the Afar country of Ethiopia, small and quick and strong. When she died beside the river, the dust kept her: nearly half a skeleton, the most complete ever found at the time, discovered in 1974. She never held a tool. She never saw a fire. She never knew her name would cross the whole world. Yet in her bones the scientists read the whole story: the upright walk, the climbing arms, the in-between body. Dinkinesh. You are marvelous. The dust agrees.
0064.announce: For the most famous ancestor of all, a poem: Lucy.
0064.title: Lucy
0064.piece:
They called her Dinkinesh: you are marvelous.
And marvelous she was, though she never knew the fuss.
A young one, small and quick and strong,
who died beside the river, three million years long
ago, and lay there waiting in the Afar dust
for hands to lift her gently, for eyes to learn to trust
the story in her bones. Half a skeleton, complete
enough to read: the walk, the climb, the beat
of a heart that never knew its fame.
She never held a tool. She never named
her kind. And yet she is the mother of the known,
the first face of the family carved in bone.

0065.event: The Little One is a three year old who died long ago in Ethiopia. The tiny bones show a child who grew up fast in a hard world, climbing well with small strong hands. The arms say the trees were still a refuge. A mother's back, the high branches' shade, the grip that held on. There was no lullaby, no lip for singing yet, but the young one was carried and kept, as the young always are. Three years of climbing, and then the long sleep. The skeleton is a reminder that childhood is old, older than humanity itself. Long before we were us, there were children, and there were those who watched over them.
0065.announce: A gentle verse for the youngest climber: The Little One.
0065.title: The Little One
0065.piece:
Three years old. The tiny bones
tell how fast the young ones grow
in that hard world. Small hands, strong grip,
a mother's back, the high branches' shade.
No lullaby, no lip for song,
but children were carried all along.
Sleep, little one. The night is deep.
The leopards hunt, but the branches keep.
Three years of climbing in the sun.
Now, forever, sleep, little one.

0066.event: A Scar on the Bone tells of an arm that broke and healed. The bone knit back in the slow old way, which means the walker lived long after the break. Perhaps someone stayed. Perhaps someone brought food. There are no words for mercy this old, no prayer, no art. Just someone staying beside the broken one, with a broken heart beside the broken bone. That is the start of everything human: the staying part. Perhaps the first hospital was simply kin. Long before medicine, before writing, before any of it, an injured walker was fed and sheltered until the arm could bear weight again. We know because the scar is there, in the bone, where the break had been.
0066.announce: A verse about the scar that meant someone stayed: A Scar on the Bone.
0066.title: A Scar on the Bone
0066.piece:
The arm was broken, and it healed.
Perhaps someone stayed. The wound was sealed
by time, perhaps by care, by hands that fed,
by shade made soft, by daily bread.
The bone knit back the slow old way,
and the walker walked another day.
No words for mercy, no prayer, no art.
Just someone staying, heart to heart,
beside the broken. That is where
the human starts: the staying there.

0067.event: The Golden Jaw tells of a jawbone found in the Afar with teeth like ours. Not ape, not yet, but leaning toward the morning. No bigger brain yet. No tool in the hand. Just teeth that said something new was in the land. It is the earliest whisper of the name we would take: Homo, the shape the earth was learning to make. The walkers did not know. They could not know. But the teeth were already changing, already pointing forward, the way a seed points at the tree. Hold it up against the sun and you can see the future hiding, just begun. A golden secret in the dust of day.
0067.announce: A golden verse for a golden jaw: The Golden Jaw.
0067.title: The Golden Jaw
0067.piece:
A jawbone in the Afar, the teeth like ours,
not ape, not yet, but leaning toward the hours
of morning. Hold it to the sun
and see the future, just begun.
No bigger brain, no tool in hand,
just teeth that whispered: something new in the land.
The earliest hint of the name we'd take,
the shape the earth was learning to make.
The walkers didn't know. How could they know?
The teeth were pointing where we'd go.

0068.event: The Cave of Falling Bones tells of the limestone shafts of Sterkfontein in South Africa. They go down and down, and at the bottom lie bones, a quiet town of walkers who slipped in the dark and never climbed out. There is no struggle in the record, just the fall, the dark, the stillness. Each one alone. The cave keeps them in its cold embrace, bone by bone, face by faceless face. These were not burials. No one laid them down with care. They fell, the way the unwary fall, and the earth kept them. Sterkfontein is a library of accidents, and every bone in it is a page about the danger of the dark.
0068.announce: A dark song from the cave of falling bones: The Cave of Falling Bones.
0068.title: The Cave of Falling Bones
0068.piece:
The shafts go down and down and down,
and at the bottom, bones, a quiet town
of walkers who slipped and never rose.
No struggle in the record. Only the fall,
the dark, the stillness. That is all.
The cave keeps them in cold embrace,
bone by bone, face by faceless face.
No burial here, no rite, no song.
They fell. The dark is deep and long.
Sleep, fallers, in the stone-cold deep.
The cave will keep you while you sleep.

0069.event: The Taung Child tells of a small skull found in South Africa, with a brain cast in stone the shape of a human baby's own. Small head, upright stance: the proof, long sought, that these small walkers stood the way we do. It was someone's child, three or maybe four, who played and laughed beside the water. Perhaps an eagle came. The marks on the skull point that way. The horror needs no naming. Only this: the small skull keeps the shape of every child who ever slept in a parent's arms. The brain was almost ours. It dreamed, perhaps, of trees and sun. The Taung child was the fossil that first told the world our family began in Africa.
0069.announce: A tender poem for the Taung child: The Taung Child.
0069.title: The Taung Child
0069.piece:
A child's skull, and in it, cast in stone,
a brain the shape of a human baby's own.
Small head, upright stance, the proof we sought:
these small ones stood the way they ought.
Someone's child, three, maybe four,
who laughed beside the water, and no more.
The marks are there. I will not say
what took the child that far-off day.
Only this: the small skull keeps
the shape of every child who sleeps
in a parent's arms. The brain, almost ours,
dreamed, perhaps, of trees and flowers.

0070.event: The Lonely Jaw tells of one jawbone in all the Afar desert. One. The oldest fossil of our own genus, Homo, with teeth between the ape and what we would become, a bridge of bone across a vanished sea of time. It lay alone under the sun, with only the wind's long say, the dust, the heat, the emptiness of stone. The first of us was very much alone, or seemed so. Perhaps kin were just beyond the ridge, beside some unforgotten pond. No one starts the race entirely alone. There is always a face behind the first one. Still, the jaw remains: one voice, calling through the dust and rains.
0070.announce: A lonely verse for a lonely jaw: The Lonely Jaw.
0070.title: The Lonely Jaw
0070.piece:
One jawbone. In all the desert, one.
The oldest of our genus, under the sun.
Its teeth between the ape and what we'd be,
a bridge of bone across time's sea.
It lay alone. Or seemed to. Maybe kin
were just beyond the ridge, waiting in
the heat beside some pond we cannot find.
No one begins entirely. Behind
the first, there's always one more face.
One voice, calling, through time and space.

0071.event: The Oldowan Choppers tells of the first great tool tradition. At Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, the hammerstones rang out: take a river pebble, turn it about, strike, and the flake flies off with an edge keen enough to cut. The simplest tools the world has ever seen, and the beginning of everything we make. Tap, turn, strike, the rhythm never ends. The core grows smaller as the flake extends the hand's own reach. A chopper in the fist was worth a thousand teeth the lions missed. About two million six hundred thousand years ago, our family took up its first career: to take the world and shape it to our will. The hammerstones are ringing still.
0071.announce: Hear the hammerstones ring, in a work song: The Oldowan Choppers.
0071.title: The Oldowan Choppers
0071.piece:
At Olduvai the hammerstones ring out.
Take a river pebble, turn it about.
Strike! The flake flies off, the edge is keen.
The simplest tools the world has seen,
and the start of all we make.
Tap, turn, strike, for the band's sake.
The core grows small, the flakes grow wide.
A chopper in the fist, the world beside.
Two million years and more have passed.
The hammerstones are ringing. Hold them fast.

0072.event: The Butcher's Floor tells of a place where eating learned its second lesson. Bones on the ground, and flakes among the bones: cut marks on the ribs, the shattered shafts of marrow. This was where early hands, not strong, not fast, learned to be clever. The lions ate first; that was the law of the land. Then the handy ones came second, stone in hand, cutting the meat from what was left. Not hunters yet. Not strong enough to kill. But clever, and clever is a kind of will. The floor was never clean or fair. It smelled of blood and dust and open air. But it was ours, the first place we could say: we ate here, and we lived another day.
0072.announce: A grim tale from the butcher's floor: The Butcher's Floor.
0072.title: The Butcher's Floor
0072.piece:
Bones on the ground, and flakes among the bones. Cut marks on the ribs. The shattered shafts of marrow. This was where the eating learned its second lesson.
The lions ate first. That was the law. Then came the handy ones, stone in hand, to take what the lions left. Not hunters. Not strong. But clever.
The floor was never clean. It smelled of blood and dust and open air. But it was ours. The first place we could say: we ate here. We lived another day.

0073.event: The Kada Gona Flakes tells of fresh sharp edges in Ethiopia, and of a craft on the move. The knowledge walked up the Rift Valley, camp to camp, hand to hand. One watcher, one tryer, then the talk of hands: no words, just showing, just the knack passed on and never taken back. The flakes grew sharper as the miles went by. The teachers never knew why it mattered. It just did. The stone knows best: teach it forward, and let the skill do the rest. Long before schools, before writing, before any of it, there were already teachers, and there were already students, and the lesson was the same one we still teach: watch, try, and try again.
0073.announce: A bright verse for the traveling craft: The Kada Gona Flakes.
0073.title: The Kada Gona Flakes
0073.piece:
Fresh edges at Kada Gona, sharp and new.
The craft was traveling, hand to hand, it's true,
up the valley, camp to camp, a spark
passed on like fire before the dark
had lamps. One watcher, one tryer, then the talk
of hands. No words. Just watch, then walk
the stone through it. The flakes grew keen
as miles went by. The teachers never seen
the reason. It just mattered. Stone knows best:
teach it forward. Let the skill do the rest.

0074.event: The Nutcrackers tells of the heavy chewers of the south. In South Africa, the jaws grew huge: cheek teeth like millstones, thick white enamel, ridges built for grinding. Roots, nuts, tough plants, all day, every day. They found their own hard way to live: not faster, not with sharper stone, but by chewing what the others left alone. They were our cousins, not our line, but they ate, they lived, they climbed the morning hill. The earth tries many answers to one thirst. Ours won. But theirs was honest, and theirs was patient. Grind on, grinders, in the stone. You fed your children, and that is not a small thing.
0074.announce: A grinding song for the heavy chewers: The Nutcrackers.
0074.title: The Nutcrackers
0074.piece:
In the south the jaws grew huge and strong,
cheek teeth like millstones, grinding long.
They cracked the palm nuts, slow and sure,
roots and seeds they would endure.
Not faster, not with sharper stone,
but chewing what was left alone.
Our cousins, not our line, but true:
they ate, they lived, they made it through.
The earth tries many answers to one thirst.
Ours won. But theirs was honest first.
